How Shopify’s Push into AI Is Working Out
 
Plus, personal computers get more expensive, and software stocks recover
 
 
Tobias Lütke. DUSTIN CHAMBERS/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Want to know whether going all-in on AI works for a large business? Watch Shopify.

 

Most established companies have come at AI with a dip-your-toes-in-the-water approach. They fear being disrupted by AI-infused competitors. But they are also wary of changing IT systems and business philosophies that have worked for decades.

 

Shopify and its chief, Tobias Lütke, have instead plunged in.

 

Shopify was quick to develop AI tools for customers, announcing an AI assistant called Sidekick in 2023. But the company has also looked inward at its use of AI. Early last year, Lütke wrote a memo to employees that explicitly made using AI a “baseline expectation” at the company, which makes software that helps retailers set up websites, process transactions and analyze their businesses.

 

That meant a few things. Employees’ performance evaluations would include questions about their use of AI. The prototyping phases of new projects would be dominated by AI-aided exploration. And before hiring new employees, teams would have to demonstrate that they couldn’t get the job done with AI instead.

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: PWC
 
 
We Turn AI Noise Into AI Solutions
 
Everyone is talking about AI. But is any of it actually working for your business? At PwC, we help cut through the AI noise so you can solve the problems that matter.
 
Learn More  >
 
 
 

Those moves may sound unremarkable now, but they were controversial at the time. The prevailing wisdom had been that companies should provide employees with AI tools to experiment with. Integrating AI deeply into daily work largely hadn’t been a strict requirement.

 

So what have the results been?

 

Shopify’s stock hasn’t done well lately—it is down more than 15% this year, including a 7% fall in midday trading Tuesday amid a broader software selloff. And it is pricey, trading at around 57 times forward earnings.

 

From a business perspective, though, there have been gains. When AI began to take off in 2023, Shopify brought in about $7 billion of revenue. Analysts project revenue will reach more than $15 billion this year as the company grows its footprint in the U.S. and internationally. Shopify has also reduced its workforce over that time, from around 11,600 at the end of 2022 to 7,600 at the end of last year.

 

These days, Lütke is looking further into the future, preparing for a shift toward so-called “agentic commerce” where AI agents instead of humans search for and recommend products. Shopify is positioning itself at the center of that shift by offering a catalog of products offered by its merchants that OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI developers can easily tap in to for recommendations.

 

While it is still early days, Shopify President Harley Finkelstein said on an analyst call last month that AI-driven traffic and orders to Shopify stores had tripled year-over-year in the second quarter.

 

Lütke said in a post on X in April that his memo a year earlier on embracing AI was evident in the company’s products and how fast they were moving. “Everyone has agents as exoskeletons for their own creativity now and knows how to use them,” he said.

 

Whether Lütke’s all-in approach continues to work looks like a good barometer of AI’s business-transforming potential.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ AI & Business newsletter, a weekly digest to help you make sense of AI’s impact on business with news, insights and data from our global team of technology journalists. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

AI Is Driving Personal Computer Prices

 
 
ANDREW KELLY/REUTERS
 

Personal computer sales are sagging—but AI might provide a respite, at least for manufacturers’ pocketbooks. While the number of PCs sold is falling, prices are up and are projected to climb further. One reason is that HP, Dell and other PC manufacturers are souping up the computers and selling them on their proficiency with on-device AI. Another is that computer-memory costs have gone through the roof because memory-intensive AI data centers have eaten up supply.

 
 
 

The Number

 
$50 Billion
 

Valuation of China’s Moonshot AI in its latest funding round. The company is one of several in China that are challenging the most advanced U.S. model developers.

 
 
 

What the Humans Are Saying

 

“I think that’s kind of satanic.”

 

— Vice President JD Vance on AI’s tendency to agree with and flatter users.

 
 
 

AI in Charts

 
 
 
 

Software stocks have had a bumpy ride this year. In January, worries were cresting that AI was going to quickly disrupt big software companies like Salesforce and ServiceNow. The idea was that supersmart AI coding tools could replace corporate software at a fraction of the cost, leaving those incumbents in the dust.

 

That hasn’t happened, and isn’t likely to happen. One big reason is that while AI tools are great at coding, they aren’t so great at maintaining and updating software on a continuous basis—which is a huge part of what software development is all about.

 

With a couple of strong earnings reports in the books since the panic earlier this year, a recovery in software stocks is now afoot. The rise could continue, too, as more investors realize that AI disruption will take a lot longer than many people initially thought.

 
 
 

AI in the Wild

 
 
Colin Edsman at Hood Summit in September 2025. SHARIF AHAMED
 

Everyday Americans are handing over their portfolios to AI agents, potentially reshaping retail investing. Proponents argue that it gives them sophisticated analysis that would otherwise only be available to professionals, although skeptics worry that AI’s growing use in investing could put less-experienced investors in financial danger.

 
 
 

WSJ’s Tech: California event returns to Napa Valley Nov. 3-4. We’ll explore the latest tech industry news with NASA administrator Jared Isaacman, Ford CEO Jim Farley, Zoox CEO Aicha Evans and more. If you’re interested in attending, request an invitation.

 
 
 

Other Highlights From the Week in AI

 

• French AI developer Mistral was valued at more than $24 billion in a new funding round.

 

• The U.S. is investing $300 million in a trio of listed quantum-computing companies.

 

• Adobe named a new chief executive as it aims to transform itself in the AI era.
